title: API client cohort latency breakdown
content:
Summary:

This note summarizes an investigation into why different API client cohorts see substantially different end-to-end latency distributions (p50/p95/p99). We analyzed 15k sampled traces collected between 2024-09-01 and 2024-09-07 using the SLO-weighted trace sampler and cohort tagging by client profile. The goal: identify dominant per-stage contributors for each cohort, prioritize mitigations that reduce p95/p99 tail for our top 3 revenue cohorts, and validate changes with targeted microbenchmarks.

Key findings (high level):
- Client cohorts with short prompts but heavy concurrency (mobile app bursts) show low p50 but high p99 driven by batching wait-time variability and occasional KV-cache cold misses.
- Clients sending longer context (3–5k tokens typical) dominate model-exec time; their p95/p99 track model forward duration and GPU queuing; batching plays less of a role for long-seq requests.
- A mid-size cohort (web chat integrations using function-calls) has a bimodal latency distribution: fast path (cache warm, small batch) and slow tail (cold cache + compilation fallback on older kernel), producing a heavy p99.

Data sources and sampling:
- Trace corpus: 15,312 end-to-end traces across 7 days (9/1–9/7).
- Sampling: SLO-weighted sampler (bias towards traces near p95/p99), augmented with uniform sample of success responses to avoid overfitting to errors.
- Instrumentation: spans captured for ingress, tokenization, kv-cache-lookup, batching-wait, model-compile-check, model-exec (GPU), emit/egress. Added custom tags: client_id, client_profile, sequence_length, cache_hit(boolean), kernel_variant.

Cohort definitions (used throughout):
- Mobile-burst: mobile clients with median concurrency > 4 and median seqlen <= 256. (4,870 traces)
- Long-context: API customers with median seqlen >= 1024. (3,420 traces)
- Integrations: third-party connectors (webhooks, function-calls) moderate seqlen (256–1024) and variable payload patterns. (2,980 traces)
- Baseline: internal synthetic traffic (1–2 tokens) used for microbenchmarks. (3,042 traces)

Aggregate E2E latency by cohort (median / p95 / p99) — end-to-end wall time measured at ingress to final byte emitted:
- Mobile-burst: p50 92 ms, p95 240 ms, p99 620 ms
- Long-context: p50 380 ms, p95 950 ms, p99 1,650 ms
- Integrations: p50 150 ms, p95 420 ms, p99 980 ms
- Baseline: p50 45 ms, p95 110 ms, p99 230 ms

Per-stage decomposition (median contribution and dominant tail drivers):
- Ingress (network parse + auth): median 8–12 ms across cohorts; not a major tail contributor except rare auth rate-limit collisions for Integrations.
- Tokenization: median 3–8 ms for short seqlen, up to 60 ms for long-context; small contributor to tail except when tokenization library falls back to slower path for non-utf8 payloads (seen in ~0.7% of traces).
- KV-cache lookup: median 2 ms when warm, but cold-miss cases add 80–300 ms depending on eviction pressure and remote KVS retry; cold misses concentrated in Mobile-burst p99 and Integrations slow path.
- Batching-wait: extremely variable — median 12 ms for mobile-burst but p95/p99 spikes to 200–500 ms when burst arrivals are sporadic and batch formation waits for N/min-latency thresholds.
- Model-compile-check/kernel fallback: rare but high-impact (5–7% of long-context p99 traces). When fallback occurs we see +300–900 ms overhead. Pattern: requests hitting newer model variants on GPU with missing optimized kernels.
- Model-exec (GPU forward): dominates long-context cohort; median 320 ms for 1k tokens with p99 ~1,100 ms when combined with queuing/backpressure.
- Emit/egress: median 10–25 ms; tail correlated with network egress retries to older egress nodes in a particular AZ (investigate).

Representative per-stage p95/p99 snapshots (mobile-burst vs long-context):
- Mobile-burst p95 breakdown (example): ingress 10 ms, tokenization 6 ms, kv-cache 60 ms (tail cases), batching-wait 180 ms, model-exec 80 ms, emit 6 ms.
- Long-context p95 breakdown (example): ingress 12 ms, tokenization 40 ms, kv-cache 10 ms, batching-wait 40 ms, kernel-fallback incidence adds +400 ms for tail subset, model-exec 820 ms, emit 28 ms.

Hypotheses and root-cause threads:
1) Batching thresholds tuned for throughput are suboptimal for mobile-burst traffic shape. Current minimum batch delay (20 ms) combined with min batch size causes pathological wait states when inter-arrival variance is high => large p99.
2) KV-cache eviction policy + sharding results in cold misses for low-volume clients that suddenly spike (mobile warmups), magnifying p99 due to remote fetches.
3) Kernel variant management: newly onboarded model variants occasionally route to hosts without compiled kernels for the hardware path, causing compile fallback and long tails.
4) Long-context GPU queuing: large forwards occupy GPU for longer, and scheduling/backpressure interacts poorly with preemption settings, increasing p95/p99 under mixed workloads.

Experiments performed (and outcomes):
- Adaptive batching run (A/B): lowered min-batch-wait to 5 ms for mobile-burst cohort and deployed target-aware batching (batch-by-client-namespace). Result: mobile p95 decreased from 240 ms to 170 ms, p99 from 620 ms to 410 ms; throughput unchanged. Metric: increased small-batch GPU invocation count by +12%.
- KV-cache local prefetching: enabled client-prefetch on warmup for top-50 mobile tokens. Result: mobile p99 reduced by ~90 ms in prefetch-pop cohort; however overall memory usage increased 4% and eviction churn rose.
- Kernel prewarm job: periodic prewarm after model-variant rollout to force compile on idle GPUs. Result: eliminated ~60% of kernel-fallback cases in Integrations cohort; p99 for that cohort dropped ~180 ms.
- Priority scheduling test: small experiment giving long-context jobs a soft-priority window to reduce preemption. Result: model-exec p95 improved 12% but increased baseline queuing for short requests; tradeoffs need policy refinement.

Microbenchmarks (baseline synthetic) to validate per-stage overheads:
- Cold KV lookup (remote): avg 220 ms (std 48 ms), aligns with cold-miss tail in traces.
- Model single-forward short sequence (B1 size): 48 ms median, matches baseline.
- Long-forward 1k tokens on A100: 310–360 ms median depending on kernel variant; kernel fallback path added +450–900 ms.

Actionable recommendations (prioritized):
1) Deploy target-aware batching policies by client-profile (short-seqlen clients get low-latency batches, long-context clients batched for throughput). Rollout gamma: 10% -> 30% -> 100% over 2 weeks with telemetry.
2) Implement KV-cache prewarm strategy for top revenue mobile clients and instrumentation to detect eviction-induced cold misses per client. Short-term: selective prefetch. Long-term: adaptive shard resizing.
3) Add kernel prewarm on variant rollout jobs and improve kernel-availability metadata in routing so requests avoid hosts missing kernels (fail fast to prewarm pool).
4) Revisit scheduler preemption windows: run controlled experiments to quantify latency vs throughput tradeoffs and add per-queue soft priorities.
5) Add a slow-path trace alert that fires when batching-wait > 150 ms AND kv-cache cold AND kernel-fallback flagged — this combination currently explains ~42% of mobile p99 cases.

Open questions / follow-ups:
- Can we add a per-client SLO-aware routing policy (route some traffic to low-latency hosts even if cost higher)?
- What are the long-term memory implications of prewarming PKV entries for many clients? Need capacity model from infra.
- Is there a stable indicator in the request fingerprint that predicts kernel-fallback risk before routing?

Immediate next steps (owners assigned):
- (Aisha) Rollout target-aware batching experiment narrow cohort (mobile-burst) 10% by 9/23.
- (Evan) Implement kernel prewarm job + routing metadata changes, PR #842, QA by 9/27.
- (Sofia) Instrument eviction metrics per-client and add dashboard. Deliver initial dashboard 9/30.
- (Liam) Run scheduler preemption tabletop and propose config changes by 10/04.

Appendix: notable trace examples (ids): trace-88f4a3, trace-d1b2c9, trace-0a9f77 (linked in Confluence page).

Notes to reviewers: this doc is an in-progress field report. Numbers are derived from sampled traces (SLO-weighted) — follow-up will include full-traffic validation and cost impact estimates for prewarm/policy changes. If you have additional client cohorts to include (region-specific, enterprise dedicated capacity) call them out and we can re-run cohort tagging.
